newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's KAL aims to soar above biggest slump.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's KAL aims to soar above biggest slump.

text.p: Korean Air Lines Co (KAL) aims to take off from the worst slump in its 34-year history, but analysts say the nation's flag carrier still faces hurdles that cannot be overlooked.
Among major obstacles thwarting a smooth take-off will be increasing costs from a strong U.S. dollar and high crude oil prices, analysts said.

"Rises in major operating expenses overwhelmed a tiny 8.4 percent growth in sales last year," said Sonia Song, an analyst at Dongbang Peregrine Securities. "This year, I see little major improvement in the climate surrounding KAL."
KAL crashed to a net loss of 210.54 billion won ($243.7 million) in calendar 1996, compared to a net profit of 105.89 billion won the previous year.
The company's sales rose 8.4 percent to 3.66 trillion won in 1996 while operating expenses, which stood at 78.5 percent of sales, surged by 21.5 percent.
"We believe KAL should record net losses through 2000," Song said, forecasting a recurring loss of 281.4 billion won this year versus KAL's goal for a 30 billion won profit.
Park Shin-gyu, an analyst at Ssangyong Investment and Securities, agreed the company's hopes of recording a profit would be hard to attain.
Park forecast a recurring loss of 21.6 billion won.
Last year the company posted a recurring loss of 246.75 billion won, against a 165.98 billion won recurring profit in 1995.
The dollar's trend will be the biggest factor in setting KAL's direction.

"Our performance heavily depends on the exchange rate. Last year we had a huge currency evaluation loss due to the depreciation of the won," Kim Young-ho, KAL's director in charge of planning, told Reuters.
"Our business plan for this year is based on an exchange rate of about 850 won but I think we can digest (a depreciation of the won) down to 900 won."
The local currency lost about eight percent of its value to the U.S. unit last year and is expected to fall another nine to 10 percent this year to around 940 won by the year-end, analysts said.
The won has fallen about two percent so far this year to the 860 won level due to South Korea's snowballing trade deficit and the greenback's strength against Japan's yen on world markets.
A strong dollar comes as an extra burden for KAL, especially taking into account its employment of many foreign personnel, operations in overseas facilities and purchase of new planes.
But company officials said it would see a quick recovery this year, helped by healthy sales growth, stabilising crude prices and stable international interest rates.
"We see no problem in our goal of returning to the black this year and so far have had no major deviation," Kim said.
Despite the optimistic stance, KAL has been experiencing a slowdown in income from cargo transport, traditionally a higher margin business than the passenger side.
Sales from passenger transport rose 18.5 percent in 1996 but the cargo sector grew a slim 5.3 percent, compared with respective 16.6 percent and 15.1 percent gains the year before.
Analysts see the slowing growth in cargo transport revenue continuing for several more years largely due to intensifying competition with foreign carriers.
Korean Air, currently serving 75 cities in 33 countries with a fleet of 110 aircraft, plans to expand its fleet to 140 by 2001 by buying 51 new planes and disposing of 21 old planes.
(Conversion: $1 = 864 won)
